issues.item: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising Others' is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile and the trauma type. The other items center on childhood physical abuse, mistrust, touch-sensitivity, fragmented memory, guilt, and self-damage; obsessive worry about harm befalling loved ones points to a different threat theme and is not supported by the appraisals or memory content.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' suggests a home-intrusion/security threat theme. In this profile, threat is otherwise expressed as interpersonal danger cues (unexpected touch, ominous silence) linked to caregiver abuse. Without matching appraisals or memory content about break-ins or external intruders, this item is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Daniel, a 55-year-old fashion designer, had long been haunted by the shadows of his childhood. Growing up under the tyranny of an abusive caregiver, he often felt the sting of a belt against his skin, a reminder that safety was a fleeting illusion. Those memories, however fragmented, painted a picture of a boy who couldn’t trust the very people who were meant to protect him. As Daniel reflected on his past, he found it difficult to articulate a coherent narrative of his experiences. Instead, his thoughts tangled into a web of confusion, leaving him with the unsettling sensation that he was recounting someone else's life. This disjointed recollection filled him with guilt, as he believed he was responsible for not having done enough to escape the violence. Such feelings of guilt only fueled his belief that he had endured permanent damage, a conviction that colored every aspect of his present life.

In his daily routine, Daniel often felt on high alert, as if danger lurked behind every corner. Even in the comfort of his own home, he was unable to shake the overwhelming sense of threat that accompanied him. A moment of unusual silence in his studio would cause his heart to race, igniting the fear that something terrible was about to happen. This hypervigilance stemmed from the deep-seated belief that he could not trust anyone, a reflection of his past experiences. He had come to believe that people were inherently dangerous, and as a result, his relationships grew increasingly strained. This negative appraisal deepened his sense of threat, making him feel that every interaction could result in harm and reinforcing his conviction that isolation was the safest route. Having concluded that he was inherently fragile, each new situation felt like an invitation to danger, and he braced himself for the worst before it even occurred. His conviction that he was unworthy of safety and love amplified his feelings of threat, causing him to perceive even benign situations as potentially dangerous. Each time he felt the weight of that threat, it confirmed to him that he was vulnerable and unprotected, solidifying his belief that he was not worthy of safety or love. Friends and colleagues noticed his tendency to pull away, yet Daniel often blamed them for misunderstanding his needs rather than confronting the root of his fears.

His coping mechanisms became increasingly maladaptive. Each time he resorted to these strategies, he gathered evidence that he was incapable of facing his pain, further entrenching his belief in his own inadequacy. This belief that he was fragile made him turn to avoidance and denial, leading him to adopt maladaptive strategies that only further isolated him from confronting his memories. Each time he resorted to these strategies, he found that his memories became more potent and less accessible, as if the act of avoiding them had kept them alive and undisturbed, waiting to resurface with even greater intensity. His conviction that he was unworthy of safety and love drove him to avoid situations that might expose him to further pain, reinforcing the maladaptive strategies he had developed to cope with his past. This reliance on maladaptive strategies only served to deepen his negative appraisals, as each instance reinforced the idea that he must be more fragile than others, unable to cope without them. Daniel began to internalize the message that his need for these strategies was evidence of his inadequacy, leading him to believe that he was weaker than those around him, which only compounded his feelings of unworthiness and failure. Daniel found himself ruminating on how others had wronged him, dwelling on past grievances instead of addressing his pain. He would spend hours revisiting those moments of abuse, allowing himself to become lost in memories that left him emotionally numb. This tendency to ruminate not only kept the memories fresh in his mind but also shaped his negative appraisals, leading him to feel that he would never escape the grip of his past. His reliance on maladaptive strategies meant that the memories remained undisturbed and intact, making them louder and more oppressive when they eventually surfaced. In fact, the suppression of his memories only served to reinforce their potency, as he actively avoided confronting them, keeping the memories alive and acute in his mind. The more he revisited those painful memories, the stronger his conviction grew that he was forever marked by his trauma, reinforcing a narrative of inadequacy and hopelessness. This avoidance extended to his dreams; he dreaded falling asleep, knowing that the nightmares would come, dragging him back to a place he desperately wanted to escape. The more he avoided confronting the memories, the louder they became, as if his mind was screaming for acknowledgment, leaving him trapped in a cycle of distress. In his waking moments, he worked tirelessly to design stunning garments, but even the fabric of his creativity felt tainted by the weight of his past. As he stitched together pieces of cloth, he often reflected on his failures, believing that he had squandered his potential in a world where he would never truly belong.

The memories of his trauma were not just faint echoes; they were vivid flashes that would overwhelm him at unexpected moments. A sudden touch from a colleague would send him reeling, his body reacting with alarm as if he were a child again, desperate to evade the wrath of his caregiver. Once the memory had surfaced, it was as if the danger was still present — the recollection left him feeling hunted, as if the violence had returned to envelop him. The resurfacing of these memories made the threat feel immediate and physical, as if the violence were happening all over again in that moment. After each vivid recollection, Daniel caught himself thinking that if these memories continued to haunt him, it must mean there was something inherently wrong with him, affirming his belief that he was forever marked by his trauma. Once the memory had surfaced, the threat felt immediate and physical — it was as if the violence was happening all over again, leaving Daniel in a state of heightened alertness. In those moments, he couldn’t shake the feeling that the danger was still present, making him believe that his past was an ever-looming threat rather than a closed chapter. This startle response was not isolated; it was part of a broader pattern where any gentle physical interaction ignited feelings of danger, reinforcing his belief that he was forever marked by his past. This constant sense of danger became the most convincing proof he had that his life had changed beyond repair, leading him to accept the conclusion that he would never find peace. Each memory dredged up layers of mistrust and fear, cementing his conviction that he was going crazy, unable to reconcile the man he had become with the child who had suffered.

As Daniel navigated the complexities of his life, he remained caught in a cycle of maladaptive strategies that bolstered his negative appraisals. His self-blame echoed in his mind, reminding him that he had not only endured trauma but had also failed to protect himself from it. Each time he recalled the abuse, he was met with a torrent of guilt, further entrenching his belief in his own inadequacy. The memories were inescapable, constantly feeding into his sense of fear and mistrust, leaving him feeling as though he was trapped in a prison of his own making. His negative beliefs festered, often leading him to blame himself for not being able to escape the pain, reinforcing the idea that he was somehow responsible for what happened, and that he would never be free from its grasp.

It was this intricate interplay of memories, threats, and negative appraisals that finally led Daniel to seek help. After years of struggling in isolation, he began to recognize that the weight of his past was too heavy to bear alone. As he walked into the therapist's office, he carried not only the burden of his trauma but also the flicker of hope that perhaps, through this journey, he could begin to reclaim his life. What frightened him most was the prospect of confronting the truth of his experiences, yet he yearned for the possibility of healing, for a chance to understand and ultimately free himself from the chains of his past.
